_comment: What to call a person, when the book calls them several things.
name_in_text is a quotation from Gutenberg #103 and is never rewritten. The payload
carries both the printed spelling and a display name, and where a chapter prints two
spellings of one person it carries both of those too. John Bunsby is 'John Busby' in
chapter 24 because that is how #103 spells him there: the book is inconsistent, the
extraction is faithful, and the reconciliation belongs here rather than in the data.
Aliases match under match_key — exactly, the way Track.matches does. No substring
matching, no surname matching: 'Smith' must not fold Joe Smith the Mormon prophet
onto the Rev. Decimus Smith, who is a different man in a different chapter.
Only names the book spells more than one way are listed. Of 159 names on stage or
named elsewhere, 145 are printed one way only and need nothing; they pass through
with display = name_in_text. Curating them anyway would be a second copy of the
extraction, kept by hand, for no gain.
roles[] is the other half, and it is a list of exceptions rather than a list of
roles. The rule is that this translation capitalises a proper name, so a name that
starts lower case — 'engineer', 'conductor', 'the cabman' — is somebody the book
identifies only by what they are. That rule is right 146 times out of 159. These are
the thirteen it gets wrong: capitalised because they carry a proper adjective or name
a people, but generic all the same.
Roles are never folded across chapters. The engineer of chapter 26 is not the
engineer of chapter 34; there are nine engineers and they are nine men. Chapter 26 is
the case that proves it: Fix and a detective are both on stage, and they are not the
same person.

people.why: printed 'Phileas Fogg' 51 times and 'Mr. Fogg' 17; chapter 19 names both, and Passepartout calls him 'Monsieur Fogg' once
his full name is given once, in chapter 1, when he introduces himself
printed one way throughout; the aliases are kept in step with tracks.json, which a test checks in both directions
in full in chapters 11 to 13, shortened in chapter 14 once he is a companion rather than an introduction
all three spellings are used, and chapter 29 uses two of them in the same chapter — the one case where a fold has to keep both quotations
chapters 20 and 21 print Bunsby; chapter 24 of Gutenberg #103 prints Busby. The source is inconsistent and both spellings are kept
named in chapter 32, then by rank in chapter 33 once he has been locked in his own cabin
the acrobat troupe's proprietor, in full and then abbreviated within chapter 23
the servant dismissed in chapter 1 over the shaving water, named in full once and by surname once
chapter 3 introduces the whist players in full; later chapters use surnames
ditto. Of the five Reform Club members only Stuart and Ralph are ever printed surname-only, so only these two need folding
the clergyman of the last chapter, with and without the article

the Mormon prophet of Elder Hitch's sermon in chapter 27. Shown as 'Joe Smith' because that is what the book prints; his own name is never the display name unless the book uses it. Not folded on the surname either: Rev. Decimus Smith is a different man in chapter 9

roles.why: a post, capitalised for the adjective — chapter 6 has one at Suez

roles.name: English engineers
roles.why: a plural trade, not a person

roles.name: Hindoos or Indians
roles.why: names two peoples, and is not anybody

roles.name: Indian dancing-girls
roles.why: a group at the Bombay pagoda

roles.name: Sioux
roles.why: names a people; the attack on the train in chapter 29

roles.name: Sioux chief
roles.why: a rank within it, and the book never names him

roles.name: Yankee
roles.why: a nickname for a kind of person, not for a person

roles.name: Parsee
roles.why: names a community. Chapters 12 and 14 may well mean the same elephant guide, but the book never names him, and asserting continuity across a two-chapter gap is the invention this pipeline refuses elsewhere
